title: A Hymn for the Bell
premise: Urban explorer Zephyrine Lockridge discovers unmapped tunnels beneath her decaying hometown, documenting them obsessively as a way to impose order on a life that has never felt real. When her childhood imaginary friend, Wren, appears on her porch unchanged after twenty years, he drags her into the tunnels' true purpose: they are the throat of something beneath the town that was fed in 1974, when six people vanished and the whole community agreed to forget. The taken were not victims but payment, and one of them was Zephyrine's grandmother, whose disappearance was rewritten as an accident. To survive, Zephyrine must return what was taken — not rescue it, return it, including the truth of what her neighbors did — and the final price is her documentation, the record she built her identity upon, which the thing below demands as its last meal.
about_author: Mara Thackeray is a former municipal archivist who spent a decade cataloguing property records in small Rust Belt towns before turning to fiction. She writes horror about paperwork, memory, and the terrible things communities agree not to see.

chapters.title: The Survey That Isn't
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. She maps a storm drain that extends far past any recorded infrastructure, photographing and logging everything with ritual precision. The emotional beat is quiet compulsion: documentation as prayer, order against dread, and the first hint that the town's paper trail has been deliberately burned.

chapters.title: Wren on the Porch
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. At dawn she finds Wren — her imaginary friend from age seven — sitting on her porch steps, physically real, unaged, asking if she's ready to go back down. The beat is uncanny tenderness curdling into fear; he knows things only her grandmother could have known.

chapters.title: What the Neighbors Kept
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, intercut with 1974 newspaper fragments. She researches the year six residents vanished; every official record calls it a gas main collapse. An elderly neighbor slams the door mid-sentence. The beat is the first wall of collective silence, and the realization that forgetting was organized.

chapters.title: Down Where the Maps End
chapters.summary: Zephyrine and Wren descend together. He navigates confidently through passages no survey shows, humming a hymn she somehow already knows. The beat is wonder giving way to violation: the tunnels are older than the town, and they have been maintained.

chapters.title: The Ledger Room
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Deep in the tunnels she finds a chamber lined with ledgers — decades of handwritten entries recording names, dates, and payments made to 'the congregation below.' Her grandmother's name appears in 1974, listed under 'received.' The beat is horror reframed as bookkeeping.

chapters.title: Six Names, One Lie
chapters.summary: Dual POV: Zephyrine present-day, her grandmother Ruth in 1974 flashbacks. Ruth discovered the ledger first and tried to expose it; the town chose the thing below over her. The beat is grief weaponized — Zephyrine realizes her family was sacrificed by consent, not chance.

chapters.title: The Congregation Below
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Living townspeople appear in the tunnels at night — respected citizens, some still in office — leaving offerings and reading entries aloud. They don't see her; Wren shields her. The beat is the sickening intimacy of recognizing faces from grocery stores and funerals.

chapters.title: Time Owes Interest
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, finally. He explains what he is: a debt-collector shaped like a child's comfort, bound to the family until the account settles. The 1974 payment bought the town fifty years; the term ends this month. The beat is betrayal braided with loyalty — he protected her so she could pay.

chapters.title: Everything I Documented
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. She reviews her own tunnel photographs and finds figures in the backgrounds she never saw while shooting — Ruth among them, watching across fifty years. The beat is vertigo: her archive was never observation; it was summons.

chapters.title: The Man Who Signed
chapters.summary: Zephyrine confronts Harold Voss, 89, the last living signatory of the 1974 agreement. He doesn't deny it; he explains it — jobs, drought, a dying child — and asks her who she'd sacrifice. The beat is moral vertigo; his logic almost lands.

chapters.title: Ruth's Last Entry
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV, 1974, complete flashback. In her final hours she hid a page of the ledger inside a church hymnal and taught young Zephyrine a song without knowing why. The beat is tragic agency: even consumed, she left a thread.

chapters.title: Hymn in a Hymnal
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. She finds the hidden page in the abandoned church where her grandmother once sang: proof the thing below can be named, and naming binds it. The congregation notices the theft immediately. The beat is fragile hope with a countdown attached.

chapters.title: They Burn Archives Too
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Her apartment is ransacked; her hard drives are gone; Voss offers her money and silence in exchange for the page. Wren warns her the town will choose again, exactly as it did in 1974. The beat is isolation — loyalty tested against truth.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The thing below speaks through him: return the page, take Ruth's place willingly, and the town — including everyone she loves — gets another fifty years. The beat is temptation rendered personal; the deal is genuinely good, which is the horror.

chapters.title: Fifty More Years
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. She nearly accepts. She visits her mother, who has spent her life half-hollowed by an unexplained grief, and understands the cost compounds down generations. The beat is refusal born of love rather than courage.

chapters.title: Reading Aloud
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Instead of returning the page quietly, she photocopies it and mails copies to every household in town, then reads the full ledger aloud in the town square at night. The congregation scatters; the thing below stirs. The beat is defiant exposure — justice outside any law.

chapters.title: What Comes Up
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs, fragmented. The tunnels open upward; the town experiences one shared night of everything forgotten surfacing — Ruth's voice, the vanished six, every suppressed memory. Some residents break; some kneel; Voss dies clutching his signature. The beat is reckoning as weather.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Zephyrine and Wren descend for the last time. She understands now: the debt isn't the page or a body — it's the truth itself, withheld for fifty years. She must give the account back, all of it, publicly and completely. The beat is grim clarity before the climax.

chapters.title: The Last Meal
chapters.summary: Climax, Zephyrine's POV. In the ledger room she feeds the thing below the only currency it truly wants: her complete documentation — every photo, log, and recording of the tunnels, her twenty-year archive of ordered certainty. It takes her records instead of her life, but demands Wren as binding collateral. The beat is sacrifice of selfhood.

chapters.title: Goodbye Is a Kind of Payment
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Wren dissolves into the settled dark, finally off the clock, whispering the hymn complete at last. The tunnels begin collapsing behind her as she climbs toward gray morning light. The beat is grief that is also release.

chapters.title: The Town That Remembers
chapters.summary: Epilogue-style, rotating brief POVs. Months later: the town holds its first memorial for the six, ugly truths aired in public hearings, some families shattered, some healed. Zephyrine keeps no records anymore; she trusts memory now. The beat is bruised communal repair.

chapters.title: A Hymn for the Bell
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, final chapter. At Ruth's belated funeral, the restored church bell rings the tune Zephyrine learned as a child, and for one moment she feels small hands hold hers — there and gone. She sings along, undocumented, unarchived, remembered. The beat is quiet grace earned at cost.
